title: Measure worker SQLite contention before changing transport lock duration
body:
## Desired outcome

Establish whether shared SQLite write-lock windows cause enough cross-device or hook blocking to justify a concurrency redesign. Produce measured synthetic evidence and a proceed/defer decision before proposing shorter transactions.

## Evidence

At `97b6b37fcbf93061adda9afab253517cee24996e`, [the worker send phase](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/blob/97b6b37fcbf93061adda9afab253517cee24996e/bridge/bridge.py#L974-L1018) and [Execution.call](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/blob/97b6b37fcbf93061adda9afab253517cee24996e/bridge/controller_state.py#L198-L225) retain immediate transactions across transport calls. [ADR 0010](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/blob/97b6b37fcbf93061adda9afab253517cee24996e/docs/decisions/0010-per-device-worker-and-nl22.md#L27) accepts these windows and gives workers a bounded wait. Commit `dd7d531` introduced [controller-read contention coverage](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/blob/97b6b37fcbf93061adda9afab253517cee24996e/tests/test_controller_state.py#L166-L215).

This establishes a contention mechanism and a prior mitigation. It does not establish unacceptable installed latency or prove that releasing locks improves the system safely.

## Scope and stop condition

A bounded measurement/design investigation using isolated SQLite, synthetic tasks and fake transport. Exercise concurrent device workers, hook admission and controller reads with short sends, delayed sends, transport timeout/failure and restart. Record lock wait separately from end-to-end operation latency.

Preserve the production implementation. Scratch experiments must not contact a device or installed database.

Stop with measurements, their limitations, and a reasoned defer/proceed decision. If evidence does not justify added complexity, retain the current locking design. No lock-release implementation is part of this issue.

## Acceptance criteria

- AC1: Record the source revision, Python/SQLite versions, transaction/journal settings, harness procedure, controlled send delays, concurrency and repetitions. Report observed waits, admission/processing latency and timeouts; distinguish hook admission from worker execution and controller reads.
- AC2: Compare healthy, delayed and failing device cases, including one slow device while another worker and a hook need state. Separate transport time from SQLite contention.
- AC3: State what counts as a material problem and why, without presenting a synthetic threshold as installed acceptance. A physical or installed claim requires separately authorized evidence.
- AC4: If proposing shorter locks, define when a send becomes irrevocably in flight, what cancellation/revocation/mode changes can still prevent, and how crash uncertainty and partial sends are journaled. Explain how the per-device exclusive worker lock remains effective.
- AC5: Specify deterministic regression scenarios for concurrent workers, cancellation between operations, crash-before/after-send windows, partial success, holds and no automatic replay. Existing recovery tests remain required.
- AC6: Record a proceed/defer decision. Proceed requires a separately scoped implementation issue, significant concurrency design, affected OpenSpec scenarios and an explicit revision of ADR 0010's locking choice; completing this investigation does not require that change.

## Verification approach

Use barriers/events and bounded waits in a fake-transport harness. Preserve the uncertainty/restart cases in `tests/test_controller_worker.py`, the contention cases in `test_controller_state.py`, and per-device ownership tests. Keep receipts and raw synthetic measurements inspectable. Do not add a production benchmark service or require a new database engine.

## Dependencies and readiness

Lower priority than the configuration, frontend and render-input boundaries. No code refactor is required to measure the current behavior. Coordinate with #129 (worker transaction ownership) so a behavior-preserving cleanup is not confused with a lock-duration change. Refresh active worker fixes before any later implementation.

#90 changes shared-feed wake-up latency; #124 measures browser rendering cost. Neither measures this database-lock question.

## Delivery target

Measurement report and design disposition on this issue only. No implementation, installation, live database access or physical-light operations.

## Work assessment

Delivery assessment for [agent-device-hub#252](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/252) on 2026-09-25, from this story's text, comments and recorded dependencies. It adds only ratings the story did not already record; readiness, labels and status are unchanged.

- **Complexity: medium.** An isolated harness simulating concurrent workers, hooks and reads.
- **Uncertainty: medium.** Whether contention matters is the open question.
- **Impact: low.** Synthetic measurement only.

title: Retire the legacy Windows runtime from source
body:
## Outcome and real setup

One operator, the Linux runtime under `~/.local/share/codex-nanoleaf`, and the devices registered there. The source no longer carries a Windows runtime: no PowerShell installer or tray, no WSL-to-Windows forwarding, no Windows MCP helper, and no documentation or specification that presents a Windows installation as supported. The Linux runtime's behavior, state ownership, and light writer are unchanged.

Excluded: the Windows browser and Codex Desktop stay as clients; the runtime keeps reading Codex Desktop's mounted JSON read-only. Decommissioning the retired Windows installation on the PC is a separate owner task. The sign-in availability decision and the Lively disposition are separate decision issues.

## Evidence

Source baseline: `3e6aa99813d43e4105017ec92c6a9e93c285a2cb` (2026-09-24). The Linux runtime has owned the lights since [#54](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/54) and [#55](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/55); the legacy hooks were removed in [#89](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/89). Nothing in Git removed the Windows path:

- Windows-only files: `bridge/install-modes.ps1`, `bridge/remove-modes.ps1`, `bridge/tray.ps1`, `bridge/tray-icon.ps1`, `bridge/tray-icon.ico`, `bridge/assets/tray-icon-source.png`, `bridge/backup_install.py`, `scripts/build-tray-icon.py`, `tests/test_tray_icon.ps1`, `tests/test_controller_install.ps1`. None runs in CI: `.depot/workflows/ci.yml` is Linux-only and the Windows job in [`.github/workflows/ci.yml`](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/blob/3e6aa99813d43e4105017ec92c6a9e93c285a2cb/.github/workflows/ci.yml#L50-L52) belongs to a disabled workflow.
- Windows branches in `bridge/bridge.py`: [`windows_path` and `data_dir`](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/blob/3e6aa99813d43e4105017ec92c6a9e93c285a2cb/bridge/bridge.py#L48-L59), [`hook_command` writing `commandWindows`](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/blob/3e6aa99813d43e4105017ec92c6a9e93c285a2cb/bridge/bridge.py#L1065-L1099), [the PowerShell remover in uninstall](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/blob/3e6aa99813d43e4105017ec92c6a9e93c285a2cb/bridge/bridge.py#L1474-L1476), [the WSL-to-Windows forwarding block in `main`](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/blob/3e6aa99813d43e4105017ec92c6a9e93c285a2cb/bridge/bridge.py#L1521-L1533), and [the `tray` command](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/blob/3e6aa99813d43e4105017ec92c6a9e93c285a2cb/bridge/bridge.py#L1596-L1602). Smaller `os.name == 'nt'` branches sit in `project_map.py`, `shared_input.py`, `wall_server.py`, and `devices.py`.
- MCP: the [`wsl-helper` transport](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/blob/3e6aa99813d43e4105017ec92c6a9e93c285a2cb/mcp/src/config.ts#L13), `mcp/windows-controller-http.py`, `mcp/tests/wsl-helper-probe.mjs`, `mcp/tests/windows-controller-fixture.mjs`, `tests/test_mcp_helper.py`, and the `windows.json` and `wsl.json` examples. The installed Linux configuration names its transport `windows-http`, kept by ADR 0007 as a compatibility identifier.
- Specifications: [`protected-controller-api` "Installed WSL command dispatch"](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/blob/3e6aa99813d43e4105017ec92c6a9e93c285a2cb/openspec/specs/protected-controller-api/spec.md#L59-L67), [`local-mcp-bindings` "Bounded Windows and WSL transport"](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/blob/3e6aa99813d43e4105017ec92c6a9e93c285a2cb/openspec/specs/local-mcp-bindings/spec.md#L54-L72), and [`integration-settings-api` retained Windows ownership](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/blob/3e6aa99813d43e4105017ec92c6a9e93c285a2cb/openspec/specs/integration-settings-api/spec.md#L47).
- Decisions: ADRs 0005, 0006, and 0007 each say legacy Windows installations retain Windows forwarding.
- Documentation: `README.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `bridge/README.md` (tray introduction, PowerShell fresh setup, bundled Windows Python hooks), `docs/development.md` (Windows upgrade, portability limits), `docs/controller-api.md`, `docs/local-mcp.md`, `docs/claude-code.md`, `.codex/README.md`, and the scope-defaults sentence in `docs/sdlc.md` that still lists legacy Windows installations as supported.

## Smallest useful implementation

Delete rather than abstract. One PR, or a short sequence on one branch, that:

1. Removes the Windows-only files and the Windows job from the disabled Actions workflow.
2. Removes the Windows branches from the bridge modules: forwarding, `commandWindows`, the tray command, the PowerShell remover, `windows_path`, and the `LOCALAPPDATA` data directory. Keep the `/mnt/c` state-directory guard in `enrollment.py` and the Linux installer's filesystem checks; they protect the Linux runtime.
3. Removes the `wsl-helper` transport, helper, fixtures, and Windows examples from `mcp/`. Renames the direct transport to a platform-neutral identifier and keeps `windows-http` as an accepted alias so the installed `mcp-config.json` keeps working after a later upgrade.
4. Adds an ADR with the next available number (ADR 0011 is taken by the sign-in availability decision from #133, so expect 0012) superseding the Windows ownership and forwarding clauses of ADRs 0005 to 0007, and records the remaining Windows touchpoint: read-only access to Codex Desktop's mounted JSON.
5. Updates the three specifications through the issue-linked OpenSpec change: drop the WSL dispatch scenario, replace the Windows and WSL transport requirement with the Linux loopback requirement, and remove retained Windows ownership. `linux-runtime` keeps its WSL-lifetime statement until the sign-in decision issue changes it.
6. Sweeps the documentation listed above so Linux is the only supported installation. Keep `docs/hardware-validation.md` with a short note that it records the retired Windows acceptance. Note in `docs/linux-install.md` that the shared monitor hook registered in the Windows Codex home carries a Linux command and only fires for tasks running in WSL.
7. Adjusts tests: remove `sys.platform == 'win32'` skips, the WSL forwarding test in `tests/test_controller_cli.py`, and the `commandWindows` fixtures; keep the mounted-drive rejection tests.

Dependencies: none required. Shared-file coordination with [#118](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/118) on `bridge/bridge.py` and `bridge/install_linux.py`; #118's AC4 and AC6 assume two installation paths and Windows PowerShell packaging checks, so whichever lands second reconciles those criteria. Preferred order: this issue before #118's packaging step, because it leaves fewer files to move.

## Behavior and protections to preserve

- The installed Linux runtime, its state directory, hooks, four user services, ports, and credentials are not touched by source delivery.
- One authoritative state owner and one light writer per device. Runtime SQLite is never placed on a Windows-mounted path.
- Every documented Linux CLI command and argument, `hooks register` and `hooks remove` for the legacy rollback path, controller and MCP authentication, and browser Host, Origin, and edit-token checks.
- Task and scene state, pulse epochs, reservations, and preferences are unaffected; no schema change.
- The demo and test suites keep running without a device or credentials.

## Observable acceptance and planned evidence

Delivery target: source-only.

- AC1: No tracked `.ps1` file, no `commandWindows`, no `python.exe` or `powershell.exe` reference, and no `os.name == 'nt'` branch remain outside the Windows-mount guards. Evidence: a recorded `git grep` inventory at the delivery revision.
- AC2: An installed-style Linux runtime copy built by `install_linux.py` from the delivered file list starts the map, controller, and MCP host with fake transport. Evidence: the existing isolated Linux runtime tests.
- AC3: An MCP configuration using the old `windows-http` identifier and one using the new identifier both pass validation and reach a fake controller. Evidence: `mcp/tests/config.test.mjs` and `transport.test.mjs`.
- AC4: The three affected specifications validate, and every retained requirement in them still has a passing test. Evidence: `npm run check:workflow`, plus the spec-to-test mapping in the PR.
- AC5: `python3 scripts/check.py`, `npm run test:browser`, `npm run test:mcp`, `npm run check:workflow`, and `npm run test:workflow` pass on Depot CI at the head commit. Record the suite count.
- AC6: The superseding ADR exists with the next available number, the documentation sweep leaves no page describing a Windows installation as supported, and the OpenSpec change is archived on the delivery branch. Evidence: inspection in independent review.

## Meaningful deferrals

- Running the Python suite on native Windows is no longer claimed. Lost: nothing CI checks today. Alternative: WSL. Revisit trigger: a second developer on native Windows.
- Upgrading a legacy Windows installation is no longer possible from source. Lost: the documented `install-modes.ps1` path. Alternative: the fresh Linux installation already in use. The retired installation is decommissioned under its own issue.
- The hub's `docs/architecture.md` still describes a legacy Windows route. Owner: the hub; update it when a guide change is in scope, per the work-guide procedure.

## Assessment

Planning stage, source `3e6aa99`, 2026-09-24, session reasoning setting high.

- Assumptions: one operator; the Linux runtime is the only active installation (confirmed on the PC: Windows tray, worker, hooks, and shortcuts are gone, four Linux user services run). The Windows install directory still exists but is idle.
- Complexity medium: many files across bridge, MCP, specs, ADRs, and docs, but each change is a deletion with an existing test boundary. Uncertainty low: the inventory above is complete at the baseline. Impact medium: the removed path is already retired, the installed runtime is untouched, and the MCP alias avoids a configuration break; rollback is a revert.
- Cuts: Windows developer support (unnecessary capability, CI is Linux-only) and the Windows upgrade path (deferred behind decommissioning). No required protection is removed.
- Readiness: ready. Reassess if #118 lands first, if the sign-in decision selects a Windows-side launcher that needs repository files, or if a Windows installation turns out to still be active.
- Review: standard independent Standards and Specification reviews. No UI change expected; if `wall.html` or `prism.js` need edits, UI approval applies.


## Related issues

- [#132](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/132) decommissions the retired Windows installation on the PC (owner task, independent).
- [#133](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/133) decides sign-in availability of the Linux runtime; this issue must not add a launcher.
- [#134](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/134) decides the Lively wallpaper issues.
- [#118](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/118) shares `bridge/bridge.py` and `bridge/install_linux.py`; reconcile its AC4 and AC6 with whichever lands second.

title: Decommission the retired Windows installation on the PC
body:
## Outcome and real setup

One operator on the PC. The retired Windows installation and the Windows-side registrations left over from its era are gone, so the Linux runtime is the only installation, no second copy of the device token exists, and Codex and Git no longer point at Windows-side paths. The Linux runtime and its data are untouched.

This is an owner task on the machine, not source delivery. It does not change lights, the Linux runtime, or any repository file. Source removal is [#131](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/131).

## Evidence

Observed on 2026-09-24 from a WSL session on the PC:

- `%LOCALAPPDATA%\CodexNanoleaf` still exists with 43 entries: `config.json` holding the device token, `status.sqlite` with task history and the controller credential ledger, `layout.json`, scene state, eight `backup-*` folders, and earlier `bridge.py.before-*` copies. No Windows worker, map server, controller, or tray process is running, and no Startup or Start Menu shortcut remains.
- The Windows Codex `hooks.json` no longer references the bridge. Its `config.toml` still trusts three temporary `nanoleaf-windows-acceptance` and `nanoleaf-live-client` directories and the 2026-09-07 orchestration project folders.
- `git worktree list` in the source checkout shows three registrations on the Windows drive for merged branches: `feat/larger-tray-icon`, `codex/gh-2-shared-skills`, and `codex/gh-28-hub-controller-api`.
- The WSL Codex `device-development` permission profile still grants write access to the Windows install directory.

## Smallest useful implementation

Manual steps by the owner, outside a restricted task terminal, in this order:

1. Confirm the Linux runtime is healthy: `nanoleaf status`, the four user services active, and the wall map reachable.
2. Decide what to keep from the Windows database. The Linux installation deliberately imported nothing ([ADR 0007](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/blob/main/docs/decisions/0007-linux-runtime-ownership.md)); if any Windows-era task history or controller receipts matter, copy `status.sqlite` with the SQLite backup API to a private archive first.
3. Revoke or confirm revoked the controller credentials recorded in that database (the 2026-09-08 acceptance revoked its test principals; check `controller_credentials` for anything else), then delete the directory, including the token copy and backups, or move it to a private archive outside any synced folder.
4. Remove the stale worktree registrations with `git worktree remove` on each path, then `git worktree prune`, only after confirming each branch is merged and no session is using the path. Delete the merged local branches if wanted.
5. Remove the trust entries for the temporary acceptance directories from the Windows Codex `config.toml`, and remove the Windows install directory grant from the WSL `device-development` profile. Source tasks need no installed directory.
6. Record what was archived, what was deleted, and the dates in this issue.

Dependencies: none. Independent of #131.

## Behavior and protections to preserve

- The Linux runtime's state directory, credentials, hooks, services, and the shared monitor are not modified.
- Unrelated Codex projects, hooks, MCP entries, and other applications' Startup items stay as they are.
- Other sessions' worktrees under `.local/worktrees` and the hub's worktrees are not touched.
- No light request is sent.

## Observable acceptance and planned evidence

Delivery target: includes installation and its verification; owner is the repository owner.

- AC1: `%LOCALAPPDATA%\CodexNanoleaf` no longer exists, or exists only as a private archive without `config.json`. Evidence: directory listing recorded in a comment without private paths.
- AC2: `git worktree list --porcelain` shows no path on a Windows drive. Evidence: the command output.
- AC3: The Windows Codex `config.toml` has no trust entry for a `nanoleaf-*` temporary directory, and the WSL `device-development` profile has no Windows install grant. Evidence: `grep` output with account names redacted.
- AC4: `nanoleaf status` and the wall map still work afterwards. Evidence: command output and a manual check.

## Meaningful deferrals

- Windows-era task history is not migrated. Lost: old task records and receipts that the Linux runtime never had. Alternative: the private archive from step 2. Revisit trigger: a request to see pre-cutover history.
- The Codex Desktop `.codex` JSON files on the Windows drive stay, because the runtime reads them.

## Assessment

Planning stage, observation date 2026-09-24, session reasoning setting high.

- Assumptions: one operator; the Linux runtime is the sole installation; no Windows process depends on the directory (verified: none running, no shortcuts). Unknown: whether any Windows-era history is wanted, resolved by step 2.
- Complexity low. Uncertainty low. Impact high: deleting the directory is irreversible and it holds a credential and task data, so the archive step is the recovery evidence the scope defaults ask for.
- Cuts: no migration tooling (unnecessary capability; a manual copy suffices).
- Readiness: backlog until the owner schedules it. Reassess if a Windows installation is found active or if the Codex profile is still needed for a Windows-side acceptance.

title: Decide how the Linux runtime becomes available at Windows sign-in
body:
## Outcome and real setup

One operator on the PC, the Linux runtime in WSL, and its registered devices. The decision settles how the lights and the shared monitor become available after a Windows sign-in or reboot without the operator opening a WSL terminal, or records that manual start is accepted. The result is an ADR and, if a launcher is chosen, one follow-up implementation issue.

Excluded: hub hosting work itself ([agent-device-hub#42](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/42) Docker on the PC, [agent-device-hub#44](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/44) dedicated server) and any change to the runtime's state ownership.

## Evidence

Observed on 2026-09-24. The Windows tray used to start at sign-in and launch the worker; it is gone. The four Linux user services start when the Ubuntu distribution boots, but nothing starts the distribution: the Windows Startup folder has no WSL entry and no scheduled task references WSL or the runtime. Until something opens the distribution, hooks, the wall map, the controller, and the hub feed are all unavailable. [ADR 0007](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/blob/main/docs/decisions/0007-linux-runtime-ownership.md) and the [`linux-runtime` specification](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/blob/3e6aa99813d43e4105017ec92c6a9e93c285a2cb/openspec/specs/linux-runtime/spec.md#L56-L58) accept this deliberately: availability follows WSL lifetime, with no Windows startup automation. The operator's stated direction since then is to remove Windows-native components, so the gap needs an explicit choice.

## Options to decide

1. One Windows-side launcher: a Startup shortcut or scheduled task that runs `wsl.exe -d <distro>` with a no-op command at sign-in, so systemd starts the services. Smallest change; it is a single Windows artifact outside this repository and would be documented as the one accepted exception. WSL idle shutdown must be disabled or the services stop again.
2. Accept manual start and make it visible: no launcher; the wall map and hub show the runtime as unavailable and the operator opens WSL when needed. No Windows component, but hooks fire into nothing until then.
3. Move hosting off WSL: fold this into the hub's Docker or dedicated-server plans. Removes the dependency on WSL lifetime and the PC's sign-in, at the cost of waiting for those deliveries. Docker Desktop on the PC has the same sign-in dependency unless it autostarts.

## Smallest useful implementation

Choose an option, record it in an ADR (next available number) with the reason and the accepted Windows-side exception if any, and update the `linux-runtime` specification and `docs/linux-install.md` sentence on availability. If option 1 is chosen, open one implementation issue for the launcher and its runbook; the launcher is an owner installation step, not source.

Dependencies: none. Related: [#131](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/131) removes the Windows runtime from source and should not add a launcher. [#134](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/134) decides the Lively issues, whose #13 overlaps this decision.

## Behavior and protections to preserve

One state owner and one light writer per device; no second runtime starts because of a launcher. The Linux services keep their explicit start and stop commands. Nothing here changes hooks, credentials, or task and scene state.

## Observable acceptance and planned evidence

Delivery target: source-only for the ADR and documentation; any launcher is a separate owner installation.

- AC1: An ADR states the chosen option, the rejected options, and the accepted Windows-side boundary. Evidence: the document in independent review.
- AC2: The `linux-runtime` specification and `docs/linux-install.md` describe availability consistently with the decision. Evidence: `npm run check:workflow` and inspection.
- AC3: If a launcher is chosen, a follow-up issue exists with its own acceptance: after a sign-in, `nanoleaf status` answers without a manual WSL start.

## Meaningful deferrals

- Hosting off the PC stays with the hub issues.
- Automatic recovery after WSL crashes or updates is not in scope; manual restart remains the alternative until a hosting move.

## Assessment

Planning stage, observation date 2026-09-24, session reasoning setting high.

- Assumptions: one operator; the PC is the host; the distribution is not started by anything else at sign-in (verified). Unknown: how often the operator reboots and whether occasional manual starts are acceptable.
- Complexity low. Uncertainty high: this is an owner decision, not a technical question. Impact medium: the choice determines whether the lights and monitor work after every reboot.
- Readiness: needs the owner's decision; blocked on it. Reassess when the hub hosting issues become ready.

title: Decide the disposition of the Lively wallpaper issues
body:
## Outcome and real setup

One operator on the PC with the Linux runtime and a Windows desktop. The five Lively wallpaper issues ([#10](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/10), [#11](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/11), [#12](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/12), [#13](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/13), [#14](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/14)) either continue with a stated boundary or close as superseded. Their labels and bodies are updated to match, so the backlog stops carrying Windows-runtime assumptions that no longer hold.

## Evidence

Observed on 2026-09-24. Lively Wallpaper is a Windows application; #13 in particular plans a Windows sign-in integration and a Windows runbook, and #10 through #14 were written while the bridge ran on Windows. Since then the runtime moved to Linux ([ADR 0007](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/blob/main/docs/decisions/0007-linux-runtime-ownership.md)), the operator asked to remove Windows-native components, and the wall map is now served from WSL on a fixed port and forwarded to the Windows loopback by WSL itself. #11's original problem, a map port that changed at startup, no longer exists on Linux. The ambient view ([#16](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/16)) and live rendering ([#17](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/17)) do not depend on Lively.

## Options to decide

1. Close #10 to #14 as superseded. Lively was a way to keep the map on a monitor; a browser kiosk window or the future ambient view can do that without a Windows integration in this repository. Lost: nothing delivered; the investigation never started.
2. Keep Lively as a browser client only. #10 and #12 continue (a Windows app rendering a page the Linux runtime serves is a client, like Edge). #11 is rechecked against the fixed Linux port and probably closes. #13's sign-in integration is folded into [#133](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/133) or dropped, since it is the one piece that puts Windows automation in this project. #14 stays blocked behind them.

## Smallest useful implementation

Choose an option and apply it to the five issues: close with a reason and a link here, or rewrite scope and dependencies to the client-only boundary and remove the Windows-runtime wording. Record the boundary in the same ADR as #133 if both are decided together, otherwise in a comment on this issue. No source change.

Dependencies: none required. Preferred order: decide alongside [#133](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/133), because #13 overlaps it.

## Behavior and protections to preserve

The wall map's browser Host, Origin, and edit-token checks and its inspection-only intent for persistent displays. Nothing here changes the runtime.

## Observable acceptance and planned evidence

Delivery target: tracker-only.

- AC1: Each of #10 to #14 is closed with a stated reason or has an updated body and labels matching the chosen boundary. Evidence: issue readback.
- AC2: No open issue in this repository plans a Windows-side installation or sign-in integration unless the sign-in decision accepted one. Evidence: an issue search recorded here.

## Meaningful deferrals

A persistent-display solution on Linux is not designed here; #16 and #17 own that direction.

## Assessment

Planning stage, observation date 2026-09-24, session reasoning setting high.

- Assumptions: one operator; Lively has no delivered work in this repository (verified: all five issues are backlog, four blocked). Unknown: whether the operator still wants the map as a wallpaper at all.
- Complexity low. Uncertainty high: owner preference. Impact low: tracker changes only, reversible by reopening.
- Readiness: needs the owner's decision; blocked on it.

comments.body:
Decision recorded by the owner on 2026-09-24: close #10 to #14 as superseded (option 1).

Readback:
- #10, #11, #12, #13, #14 are CLOSED with reason `not_planned`, each with a comment linking here, [#131](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/131), [ADR 0007](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/blob/main/docs/decisions/0007-linux-runtime-ownership.md), [#16](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/16) and [#17](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/17). Status and blocked labels removed; `enhancement` kept.
- AC2 search: open issues whose titles mention Lively or Windows are only #131, #132, #133 and #134, all of which retire Windows components or decide their boundary. No open issue plans a Windows-side installation or sign-in integration. The sign-in decision itself is recorded on #133 (wait for hub hosting, no launcher).

The hub work guide's roadmap node for the Lively prototype will be retired in the guide refresh linked from #133.

title: Merge the wall map inspector cards and rethink reservation and override controls
body:
### Outcome and real setup

One operator, the Linux installation, the registered Lines wall (and the Light Panels once #44 lands). The wall map's default screen is a status display: the header shows Mode, the live readout and the connection pill; the wall heading and its Options menu; and one context card for whatever is selected, a Line or a task, with the task's details and Locate. Placement stays automatic. Layout switching and placement editing are secondary: they live in Options and, for reservations, halves and the task override, appear only while Project layout is active. Excluded: the device selector (#44), a new dashboard, changing the physical Locate boundary, allocation rules, per-task pinning, and the #77 compact task grid.

Evidence: reviewing the #78 candidate (PR #125) on 2026-09-24, the owner found the inspector cluttered and its reservation and override controls not useful in their current form. A read-only look at the installation the same day showed Classic layout, 15 Lines, 10 tasks, 34 projects synced from Codex, 0 reservations, 0 swapped halves and 0 overrides, with 7 of 10 tasks attributed automatically. In Classic the wall ignores reservations, which is why an earlier manual Line assignment appeared to do nothing.

### Smallest useful implementation

Decisions settled with the owner on 2026-09-24 (grill-with-docs; an ADR in `docs/decisions/` ships with the delivery PR):

1. Status display by default. Remove the Layout buttons and the Coverage select from the header. In Classic layout no reservation, half-swap or override control appears anywhere. The bridge, the CLI `style` command and the integration-settings extension keep Project layout, reservations and overrides unchanged.
2. Add a Layout group (Classic / Project) to the Options menu; Coverage appears in that group only while Project is active.
3. Merge the selection card and the task detail card in `bridge/wall.html` into one context card: Line number(s), the task's title, status, project, elapsed time and Open in Codex link when it qualifies, then Locate. Waiting tasks, Lines without a task and multi-Line selections render conditional sections; multi-Line selection stays and Locate is disabled for more than one Line.
4. While Project layout is active, the context card adds a Reserved for select above the task, applied on change to every selected Line (no Reserve button; several Lines with different reservations read "Several reservations"), and Swap halves. The map offers no per-task project override; the integration-settings extension keeps that operation for machine clients. Pending edits during a comet are unchanged. (Revised on 2026-09-24 during review of PR #137: the owner keeps reservations and drops the map's override.)
5. Remove Clear selection. Escape or a click on empty wall canvas clears the selection and returns focus to the wall heading.
6. Show the Locate explanation only in Free, under the disabled button.
7. Orientation keeps its current default and its saved per-device settings; Rotate, Flip H and Flip V stay in Options.

Vocabulary for the guide and specs: "layout" in user-facing text (code and CLI keep `style`); "reservation" for a Line saved for a project; "attribution" for the automatic task-to-project lookup and "override" for the manual one; "context card" for the merged card; "Options" for the wall's secondary controls. Prerequisites: none. Coordinate with PR #116 (#117 focus repair in the same file).

### Behavior and protections to preserve

The bridge contract: reservations by physical Line ID, the Shared pool, manual overrides, and pending edits applied after an active comet finishes, all still editable from the map while Project layout is active and from the machine API. One light writer per device; Locate remains the only physical action and stays disabled in Free; selection, opening the card, opening Options and switching layout send no request beyond the existing settings write for a layout change; the existing origin and edit-token checks. Keyboard focus through polling, including the #117 repair, the #105 stable row positions, the #108 Open in Codex link, unread state and scene state keep working. Saved reservations, half choices, overrides, orientation and colors survive unchanged.

### Observable acceptance and planned evidence

Delivery target: source-only.

- [x] In Classic the header shows Mode, the readout and the connection pill only; the context card shows the Line, the task's details and Locate; no reservation, half-swap, override or Coverage control is visible (browser check, screenshots at 390, 800 and 1440 px).
- [x] Options contains a Layout group; choosing Project sends only the existing settings request, reveals Coverage in Options and the reservation, Swap halves and override controls on the context card; choosing Classic hides them again (browser check with request recording).
- [x] The selected task's title and project appear once in the inspector outside its tile; waiting tasks, Lines without a task and multi-Line selections render correctly, with Locate disabled for more than one Line (browser check).
- [x] Escape and an empty-canvas click clear the selection and return focus to the wall heading; no Clear button remains; the Options menu still closes on Escape first when it is open (browser check).
- [x] The Locate explanation is absent in Work and Quiet and present under the disabled button in Free (browser check).
- [x] Choosing a project under Reserved for and swapping halves in Project layout still work through the existing endpoints, a rejected choice returns to the saved value, and no task override control exists in the map (browser fixtures; Python suite unchanged or passing).
- [x] Keyboard focus through polling, long titles, the #117 repair and the existing suites pass with updated fixtures.
- [x] Explicit human approval of the current UI candidate before merge.

Checks: `npm run test:browser`; `python3 scripts/check.py` (with Node 24 available); OpenSpec deltas for `wall-map-hierarchy` (header composition, Layout in Options, context card), `wall-line-identification` (context card identification, Project-only reservation controls, Reserve label) and `wall-task-inspector` (context card replaces the detail card, override only in Project layout); `npm run check:workflow` and `npm run test:workflow`; the ADR in the delivery PR.

### Meaningful deferrals

- Per-task pinning (a task on a chosen Line, freeing a Line): not wanted now; automatic placement covers 10 tasks on 15 Lines. Revisit the first time the owner wants a task on a specific Line.
- Setting a project on a task from the map (3 of 10 have no attribution today): no map control in either layout; tasks show "No project" and the machine API keeps the override. Revisit the first time a Claude Code task must sit under a project.
- Retiring Project layout from the bridge, CLI and API entirely: deferred; the UI change alone removes the clutter. Revisit if Project layout stays unused after this change lands.
- Side-by-side devices and the combined allocation pool stay with #44 and #47.

Follows #78 (PR #125). Related: #75, #117 / PR #116, #44, #105, #108, #47.

title: Customize Work-mode light colors so unread tasks stand out from the base
body:
### Outcome and real setup

One operator, the Linux installation, the registered Lines wall and, when registered, the NL22 Light Panels. In Work mode the operator can tell at a glance which Lines carry a finished task waiting for review ("ready"; the bridge calls it unread) and which are unused. The operator can also choose the colors used for the base and for each status.

Today unused Lines and read or interrupted task Lines are steady blue `#193CFF`, and unread tasks pulse between 20% and 100% of the same blue (`BASELINE` and `COLORS['unread']` in `bridge/bridge.py`). At the 30% Work brightness the unread pulse is hard to tell apart from the base. The completion comet tail is blue too, and the map draws empty Lines and unread tasks with the same `--wall-unread` token. Status colors are fixed constants in `bridge/bridge.py` and CSS tokens in `bridge/wall.html`; only project colors can be edited.

Excluded: animation style per status (#20), completion celebration choice (#19), the live renderer (#17), Free mode and the Nanoleaf app's own scenes.

### Palette and options

Default palette, accepted by the owner on 2026-09-24:

| Role | Today | New default | Suggested alternatives |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Base (unused and read Lines) | Blue `#193CFF` | Dim blue `#0A1866` (about 40% of today's blue) | Today's blue, dim warm white `#4D3F2A`, Off `#000000` |
| Working | Green `#00FF00` | Unchanged | - |
| Question | Yellow `#FFFF00` | Unchanged | Amber `#FFB000` |
| Blocked | Red `#FF0000` | Unchanged | - |
| Unread (ready) | Blue `#193CFF` | Violet `#9B30FF` | Magenta `#FF00C0`, cyan `#00E5FF`, warm white `#FFE0B0` |

Unread shares the base hue today. The fix gives Unread a hue no other role uses and makes the base dimmer than the task Lines. Violet is far from the blue base and from green, yellow and red. White is not the default because the comet head and the Locate flash are already white. Off makes task Lines stand out most but leaves a mostly dark wall, so it is offered as a swatch to try.

Customization in this issue:

1. A color choice for each of the five roles: Base, Working, Question, Blocked and Unread. Each offers the suggested swatches above and a custom color.
2. Reset colors, which restores the defaults and nothing else.
3. A warning in the Colors group when two roles are too similar to tell apart, such as Unread and Base today. It does not block saving.
4. One palette for every registered device, so Lines and Panels agree.

Where the palette applies:

- Work: the base for unused Lines and for read or interrupted task Lines; status colors for pulses and outward waves. The comet tail uses the Unread color, because the Line settles into Unread afterward. The comet head stays white.
- Quiet: the same colors, steady at 10%.
- Project layout: the status half of an unused reserved Line and empty Shared Lines use the base. Project halves keep their project colors, and animation coverage is unchanged.
- Wall map: the wall artwork and legend use the effective colors, including the Project halves sample.
- Unchanged: Free, the white Locate flash, the white comet head, the remembered scene and the steady blue fallback shown before any scene has been remembered.

### Smallest useful implementation

Store one palette in private SQLite. The worker reads it for each frame in place of the fixed `BASELINE` and `COLORS` values, and `PRIORITY` stays keyed by status. Expose the effective palette in `/api/state` and accept changes through the existing validated settings write, with the page origin and request token. Add a Colors group to the wall map's Options menu with the five choices, swatches and Reset colors, and replace the map's fixed status tokens with the effective palette. Prerequisites: none. This does not wait for #17.

Planning: an issue-linked OpenSpec change. Task-light colors have no capability spec yet, so the change migrates the relevant bridge guide contract (status table, pulses, waves, comet colors and Project halves) into a new capability spec alongside the delta. It also adds a `wall-map-hierarchy` delta for the Options group.

### Behavior and protections to preserve

The worker stays the only light writer for each device. Alert priority comes from status, not color: blocked stays on top even when set to violet. A color change applies within about two seconds without restarting pulse epochs, replaying outward waves or comets, moving tasks between Lines or releasing comet source reservations. Mode, scene selection and brightness, project colors, reservations, halves, coverage, orientation, and task and unread state are unchanged. Opening the Colors group sends no request. Invalid colors and unknown roles are rejected without a partial update. The Nanoleaf token never reaches the browser.

### Observable acceptance and planned evidence

Delivery target: source-only.

- [ ] The Options menu has a Colors group with Base, Working, Question, Blocked and Unread choices, each with suggested swatches and a custom color, plus Reset colors. Choices survive a restart (browser check; isolated persistence test).
- [ ] In Work, unused and read Lines use the base color. An unread task pulses in the Unread color, and the comet tail uses the Unread color with a white head. Working, question and blocked use their chosen colors for pulses and waves (fake-clock frame tests on `zone_color` and `effect_payload`).
- [ ] Quiet shows the chosen colors steady at 10%; Free is unchanged (frame tests).
- [ ] In Project layout the status half and empty Shared Lines use the base, and project halves keep their colors under both coverage settings (frame tests).
- [ ] With blocked set to violet and unread set to red, blocked still overrides question, working and unread in overlapping waves and comets (frame tests).
- [ ] Applying or resetting colors mid-pulse and mid-comet restarts no epoch, replays no wave or comet and changes no assignment (fake-clock test).
- [ ] With the base set to Off, unused Lines stay dark while indicators show, and the remembered scene still returns when the last indicator clears (frame and worker tests).
- [ ] The wall artwork and legend use the effective colors, and status labels stay readable whatever colors are chosen (browser check with screenshots).
- [ ] A similar-color warning appears when Unread equals Base and clears when they differ (browser check).
- [ ] Invalid hex values, unknown roles and missing request tokens are rejected with nothing applied (API tests).
- [ ] Upgrading an existing installation keeps project colors, reservations, map settings, mode and scene, and starts with the new default palette (migration test with isolated state).
- [ ] Registered Panels use the same palette for their status display (frame test with the synthetic NL22 layout).
- [ ] Explicit human approval of the current UI candidate before merge.

Checks: `python3 scripts/check.py`, `npm run test:browser`, `npm run check:workflow` and `npm run test:workflow`. A physical side-by-side check of the default Unread and Base colors on the Lines with `setup --demo` needs an explicit request and the installation owner. Record it separately from the software evidence.

### Decisions

Settled with the owner on 2026-09-24, who accepted each recommendation:

1. Unread default: violet `#9B30FF`. LED color at 30% brightness can look different from the screen. If violet reads poorly on the Lines, the owner picks another swatch; no code change is needed. The physical check is optional and needs an explicit request.
2. Base default: dim blue `#0A1866`.
3. Existing installation: adopts the new defaults on upgrade, because no status colors have been saved and today's default is the problem.
4. Relationship to #18: this issue delivers the configurable palette without waiting for #17. #18 is narrowed to keeping #17's live view consistent with this palette. #19 and #20 take their palette from this issue.

### Meaningful deferrals

- Named whole-palette presets, such as Neon or High contrast: the operator picks each color instead. Revisit if choosing colors one by one proves tedious.
- Per-device and per-project status palettes: one palette covers every device. Revisit if the Panels need different colors from the Lines.
- Palette changes from the CLI, controller API, MCP or integration settings API: the wall map is the only editor. Revisit when a native client or the hub frontend needs to show or edit colors (see #18's shared-hub note).
- The no-scene fallback blue stays as it is, because it appears only before a scene has been remembered. Revisit if it shows up in normal use.
- Animation style per status and celebration choice stay with #20 and #19.

### Assessment

Planning stage, 2026-09-24, against `main` at `7a030ac`. Assumptions from `AGENTS.md` and `docs/sdlc.md`: one operator, the Linux installation, registered Lines and Panels.

- Complexity: medium. Worker frame colors, the map's tokens and legend, stored settings and the API, the Options menu, Project halves, Quiet, the comet tail and Panels change together.
- Uncertainty: low. The decisions are settled and the approach follows the existing project-color editing. How violet looks on the physical Lines is unverified, but the Colors group lets the owner change it.
- Impact: low. The change is presentation only, the new state is additive and Reset restores the defaults. The main risks are restarted epochs and lost project colors, both covered above.
- Readiness: ready. No prerequisites; the similar-color threshold and the new capability spec's name are settled in the OpenSpec change.

Related: #18, #17, #19, #20.

## Execution recommendation

**Start with:** a one-shot session. Claude Code on Sonnet (`sonnet`) at `high` effort, or Codex on Sol (`gpt-6-sol`) at `medium` reasoning. Paste that host's prompt below. It stops once to show you the Colors group design.

**Why:** Medium complexity with low uncertainty and impact. The worker's frame colors, the stored palette, the settings API, the Options menu, the map's color tokens and a new capability spec change together, and the checks are reliable: fake-clock frame tests, isolated SQLite state, the browser suite and the owner's UI approval. title: Add an upgrade and rollback command for the Linux runtime
body:
### Outcome and real setup

One operator, the Linux installation under `~/.local/share/codex-nanoleaf`, the registered Lines wall and Panels. After a source merge, the operator runs one command from the repository checkout that upgrades the installed runtime to that revision with a backup and a verified restart, and can roll back to a backup with one command. Excluded: the retired Windows runtime, enrollment, hook changes, device commands, remote hosts and any automatic deploy.

Evidence: [the Linux guide](docs/linux-install.md) still says "there is no upgrade or rollback mechanism here", yet the installation was upgraded by hand four times in two days (gh88 and the gh98 recovery on 2026-09-24, the gh218 trial at 17:28 local, and main `7a030ac` for #78/#135/#138/#116 on 2026-09-25 at 03:39 UTC). Each run was an ad-hoc script of the same steps: stop `codex-nanoleaf-wall` and `codex-nanoleaf-controller`, stop hook-launched `bridge.py worker` processes that hold the device locks, back up `runtime/bridge` and the state-root files with a receipt, copy the `install_linux.copy_runtime` file set and the vendor tree via temp and rename, restart, and confirm every bridge process started after the newest file. Receipts live under `install-backups/`. The hand steps that went wrong or nearly went wrong: a hook can launch a worker on the old code mid-swap, the worker start-time check is easy to skip, and sequence-numbered artifacts raced between parallel PRs (ADR 0012 in #135 and #138), which a merge-step recheck would have caught.

### Smallest useful implementation

- Add `upgrade` and `rollback` subcommands to `bridge/install_linux.py`, run from the checkout: verify the checkout is clean and record `git rev-parse HEAD`; write `install-backups/upgrade-<timestamp>/` with a copy of `runtime/bridge`, the state-root files and a `receipt.json` (source revision, file hashes, services touched); stop the wall and controller services with `systemctl --user`; SIGTERM stray `bridge.py worker` processes and wait for them to exit; copy the `copy_runtime` file set and `vendor/` via temp and rename and clear `__pycache__`; install `requirements-controller.txt` into `.venv` only when it changed; restart the services; verify both are active, every bridge process started after the newest file, and `/` and `/api/state` answer on the wall port; print the receipt path. `rollback --backup <dir>` performs the same stop, copy and restart from a backup.
- Replace the guide's "no upgrade or rollback mechanism" sentence with the command, what it touches (not the MCP host, the Hub monitor, hooks or devices) and the note that the map page is read per request.
- Add one sentence to docs/sdlc.md Review and merge step 6: after main advances, recheck sequence-numbered artifacts such as `docs/decisions/` before merging.
- Prerequisites: none. Existing components: `install_linux.copy_runtime`, the systemd units, the receipts convention under `install-backups/`.

### Behavior and protections to preserve

One light writer per device: no worker runs on old code after the swap, and device locks are released before files move. Task, scene, reservation, unread, pending-edit and comet state are backed up, never modified. The MCP host and Hub monitor services are untouched. No device, firmware or router change; hooks unchanged. Receipts hold revisions and hashes only; private state stays out of Git.

### Observable acceptance and planned evidence

Delivery target: source-only for the command; its first real use is a separately authorized installation.

- [ ] In an isolated state directory with fake service and process control, `upgrade` writes the backup and receipt, replaces the file set via rename, clears `__pycache__`, restarts the services in order, and reports a stale worker when one is simulated (Python suite).
- [ ] `rollback` restores the previous file hashes from a backup (Python suite).
- [ ] The command refuses a dirty or unknown checkout and touches no state file (Python suite).
- [ ] The guide section and the SDLC sentence are updated; `npm run check:workflow` and `npm run test:workflow` pass; `python3 scripts/check.py` passes with Node 24 available.
- [ ] One authorized upgrade on the real installation records its receipt and worker verification (installation acceptance, separate request).

### Meaningful deferrals

- Automatic upgrade on merge or a CI-driven deploy: not needed for one operator; revisit if manual upgrades start being forgotten.
- Node runtime or MCP host upgrades: out of scope; revisit when the MCP host needs a new build.
- Windows: retired by #138.

Related: #78 and #135 (install receipts of 2026-09-25), Hub #218 (trial upgrade), #138, `docs/linux-install.md`.

## Work assessment

Delivery assessment for [agent-device-hub#252](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/252) on 2026-09-25, from this story's text, comments and recorded dependencies. It adds only ratings the story did not already record; readiness, labels and status are unchanged.

- **Complexity: medium.** Service stop and start ordering, stray-worker termination, an atomic file-set swap and backup receipts in one sequence.
- **Uncertainty: low.** Four manual runs, including their near-misses, already document the procedure.
- **Impact: high.** Operates the one live installation: services, device-lock release and runtime files, with rollback as the recovery path.

## Execution recommendation

**Start with:** One-shot: one session implements it directly. Claude Code on Opus (`opus`) at `high` effort, or Codex on Sol (`gpt-6-sol`) at `high` reasoning. Paste that host's prompt below. The authorized upgrade on the real installation is a separate step with the installation owner.

| Thinking level | `high` | `high` |
| Session type | One-shot | One-shot |
| Subagents | None | None |
| Reviewers | Two fresh read-only Opus (`opus`) reviewers, one for Standards and one for Specification | Two fresh read-only Sol (`gpt-6-sol`) reviewers at `high`, one for Standards and one for Specification |
| Availability | Provisional: aliases verified from this host's Agent tool on 2026-09-25; the agent cannot observe its effort level | Provisional: not inspected from Claude Code (2026-09-25); confirm the model and reasoning options in Codex first |

**Prompt (Claude Code):**

```text

State the model you are running and stop if it is not Opus; take the effort as stated rather than guessing it. Run as a one-shot session: implement it yourself without worker subagents, and use two fresh read-only Opus reviewers for deliver-work's required Standards and Specification reviews. The issue's Execution recommendation (assessed 2026-09-25) is the basis; if what you find no longer fits it, say so before changing strategy. If deliver-work isn't available here, say so and stop.

The issue's Execution recommendation (assessed 2026-09-25) is the basis; if what you find no longer fits it, say so before changing strategy. If deliver-work isn't available here, say so and stop.

**Cheaper start:** none recorded; high impact keeps the stronger capability floor.

**Why:** Four manual runs define the procedure, but the command stops and restarts the live services, terminates stray workers holding device locks and swaps the runtime files. Policy row: high complexity or impact in a bounded outcome.

title: Play custom animations for different events
body:
## Outcome

Different events play their own animation on the Lines. For example, a green sweep when CI passes, a red ripple when it fails, or a slow sunrise in the morning. The user picks which events get an animation and what it looks like.

Placeholder for future refinement. Set scope, dependencies and acceptance criteria before implementation.

## Starting point

#92 delivered `animation.play`. It has five patterns: `wave`, `gradient`, `pulse`, `breathe` and `sparkle`. Each takes 1 to 8 colors, a speed (`slow`, `medium` or `fast`), a direction (`left`, `right`, `up`, `down`, `outward` or `inward`) and a loop or play-once choice. Animations play only in Free and stay until something replaces them. The suggestions below reuse those patterns unless marked *new*.

### Suggested events and animations

| Event | Suggested animation | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CI passed on a PR | `gradient` up, green → teal, `medium`, once | Development workflow |
| CI failed | `wave` outward, red → orange, `fast`, once | Must not hide a real blocked task |
| PR merged | `sparkle`, blue, green and gold, `medium`, once | |
| Review requested or changes requested | `pulse`, purple, `medium`, a few cycles | |
| Installation or deploy finished | `wave` outward, teal → white, `medium`, once | |
| Start of day | `gradient` up, deep orange → pink → warm yellow, `slow` | Scheduled |
| Focus timer ended | `breathe`, soft green, `slow`, a few cycles | Scheduled |
| Meeting in five minutes | `pulse`, amber, `medium` | Needs a calendar source |
| End of work day | `wave` inward, warm amber → dim red, `slow`, then Free or Quiet | Scheduled |
| Device, controller or MCP error | `breathe`, dim red, `slow` | Local health events |
| Codex task completed | Covered by #19 (celebration presets) | Link, don't duplicate |
| Codex needs approval or is blocked | Covered by #20 (per-status presets) | Link, don't duplicate |

Pattern ideas that would help, each needing its own design:
- *New* `spin`: a sweep that rotates around the wall's center. The current layout surrounds its center, so this would suit it.
- *New* `chase`: a light that runs along physically connected Lines.
- *New* speed: one step faster than `fast`.

All of these must stay within the envelope #92 qualified, 20 frames per zone and 8,192 bytes, unless a live probe raises it.

## Open questions

- **Over Work status.** An animation that plays over Work status needs its own hub ADR 0005 decision, including how and when status resumes. Free-only events avoid that decision. hub [#45](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/45) records the same open question.
- **Rules.** Where do event-to-animation rules live and run without a conversation? hub #45 owns approved automation rules; this issue could own the Nanoleaf presets those rules call.
- **Restoring.** After a play-once animation, return to the scene or status that was showing before it, not to a stale snapshot. Loops need an explicit stop.
- **Precedence.** Red and yellow alerts, completed comets and unread state must never be erased or restarted. Decide what happens when two events collide, and how duplicates are rate-limited.
- **Event sources.** GitHub events need polling or a webhook. Remote ingress is deferred by hub ADR 0004. Calendar and timer sources are undecided.
- **Preferences.** Where per-event choices are stored, how they're previewed, and whether the wall map needs UI for them (a UI change needs human approval).

## Related

- #92: the typed animation command and MCP tools this builds on.
- #19 and #20: completion and per-status presets, which cover the task-lifecycle events.
- hub [#45](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/45): approved alert and device automation rules.
- hub [ADR 0005](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/blob/main/docs/decisions/0005-general-device-controls.md): Free-only content and no automatic restore.

## Guide

**Topic:** nanoleaf-presentation
**Highlight:** idea, Per-event animations such as CI passed, PR merged and start of day.
**Extends:** N92

title: Cap how fast animations can flash
body:
## Outcome and real setup

Requested animations on the Lines never flash faster than a safe rate unless the owner opts in. It is a photosensitivity safeguard that must be in place before faster speeds or new patterns land (see #151).

Measured on 2026-09-25 against the 15-Line fixture at `fast`, the worst per-Line brightness peak rate today is `pulse` at 2.0 per second. `wave` with 8 colors reaches 1.7 and everything else stays below 1. All of these are under the common 3-flashes-per-second guideline (WCAG 2.3.1), so this protects future speeds and patterns rather than fixing a current defect.

## Smallest useful implementation

- A shared check in `bridge/effects.py` that computes each Line's peak rate from the encoded frames and rejects an effect above the limit with `capacity` before queueing. This is the same admission point as the byte and frame bounds.
- A pure frame property that needs no device.
- The animation options route and `nanoleaf_animations_list` report the limit.

## Behavior and protections to preserve

- All five current patterns, at every speed, stay allowed.
- Status animations, comets and alerts are not subject to this check.
- The frame and byte bounds and the Free-only gate stay as they are.

## Observable acceptance and planned evidence

- Tests compute peak rates for every pattern, speed and color count on the fixtures, and assert that none exceeds the limit.
- A synthetic too-fast frame list is rejected before queueing and consumes no ticket.
- The options route reports the limit.

## Meaningful deferrals

- An owner opt-in to exceed the limit is deferred until someone asks for it. The manual alternative is none, by design.


## Work assessment

Planning assessment, 2026-09-25, from #92's delivery and the live session. Source-only delivery unless stated.

- **Complexity: low.** One pure function and a limit field.
- **Uncertainty: medium.** The threshold and how "flash" is measured (luminance delta, area) need an owner decision. Default proposal: at most 3 peaks per second per Line, with at least a 2:1 luminance change.
- **Impact: medium.** It is a safety property on a physical device.
- **Readiness:** deferred. The owner decision below removes the need for a cap on this installation.

## Decision (owner, 2026-09-25)

The owner is not sensitive to flashing and asked to be lax here. No flash-rate cap is enforced on this installation. The device's one-decisecond frame resolution already bounds any pattern at about 5 flashes per second, and the frame and byte bounds still apply. This story stays as an optional guard. Revisit it if someone who may be sensitive shares the room, or if the wall becomes visible to others (for example a stream or a shared space). It no longer blocks #151.

Follows #92 and complements #146.

## Guide

**Topic:** nanoleaf-presentation
**Note:** Cap how fast requested animations can flash.

title: Stop an animation and restore the remembered scene through MCP
body:
## Outcome and real setup

From Codex, "stop the animation" returns the Lines to the scene the bridge remembers (for example, Cozy Blaze at its remembered brightness) with one explicit command. After the #92 live check, stopping a looping animation took a manual `scene.activate` of the remembered scene.

## Smallest useful implementation

- The animation options route (`GET /controller/integration/v1/animations`) adds `rememberedSceneId`, the opaque ID of the remembered scene, or null when none is remembered or it is no longer advertised.
- A new MCP control tool, `nanoleaf_scene_restore`, reads that ID and sends one existing v1 `scene.activate` through the same path as `nanoleaf_scene_activate`. It never switches mode.
- No controller v1 change and no extension snapshot change (the hub validates the snapshot exactly).

## Behavior and protections to preserve

- Hub ADR 0005: this is an explicit command, and nothing restores automatically. The tool is Free-only, like `scene.activate`, and the Work/Quiet rejection message says to switch to Free.
- Scene names stay out of the shared v1 snapshot.
- The remembered scene and its brightness are unchanged by the tool; only the worker's existing restore policy writes them.
- There is one light writer.

## Observable acceptance and planned evidence

- Controller tests: the options route reports the remembered scene ID; the ID is null when nothing is remembered and null when the scene disappeared.
- MCP tests: restore sends exactly one `scene.activate` with the caller's request identity; Work/Quiet is rejected with the switch message; a null ID gives a typed failure with no dispatch.
- Live, when requested: play an animation, ask Codex to stop it, and confirm the remembered scene returns.

## Meaningful deferrals

- Restoring brightness as well as the scene is deferred. Today's Free handoff already restores it, and the #92 live check found it unchanged. Revisit if an override leaves it different.


## Work assessment

Planning assessment, 2026-09-25, from #92's delivery and the live session. Source-only delivery unless stated.

- **Complexity: low.** One read field and one tool reusing `scene.activate`.
- **Uncertainty: low.**
- **Impact: medium.** It writes to a physical device through an existing command.
- **Readiness:** ready.
- **Acceptance mapping:** controller and MCP unit tests plus the protocol test; live check optional.

Follows #92 and complements #146.

**Note:** Stop a requested animation and restore the remembered scene through MCP.

title: Add a rotating spin direction and a faster speed for animations
body:
## Outcome and real setup

Codex can play a sweep that rotates around the wall's center, clockwise or counterclockwise, and can pick a speed one step faster than `fast`. On the owner's 15-Line wall the Lines surround the centroid (angles cover the full circle), so a rotation reads clearly.

## Smallest useful implementation

- `bridge/effects.py` `phases()` gains `clockwise` and `counterclockwise`, computed from each Line's angle around the centroid. The spatial patterns (`wave`, `gradient`) accept them.
- A new speed, for example `faster`, uses a shorter keyframe step, still within 20 frames per zone and 8,192 bytes.
- Validation, the TypeScript consumer and fixtures, and the MCP enums are updated. Specs and docs follow.

## Behavior and protections to preserve

- Existing directions and speeds keep their frames byte for byte.
- Free-only gating, receipts and the single writer are unchanged.
- The faster speed may go down to the device's one-decisecond keyframe step; no flash cap applies (owner decision in #149).

## Observable acceptance and planned evidence

- Encoder tests: crest order follows angle for both rotations on the 15-Line and two-Line fixtures; the faster speed produces a shorter cycle; every combination stays within the frame and byte bounds.
- MCP tests list the new values.
- Live, when requested: play a clockwise wave and confirm the rotation.

## Meaningful deferrals

- Choosing a custom rotation center is deferred. The centroid is used. Revisit if the owner's wall shape makes it look off-center.


## Work assessment

Planning assessment, 2026-09-25, from #92's delivery and the live session. Source-only delivery unless stated.

- **Complexity: low.** Encoder and enum changes.
- **Uncertainty: low.**
- **Impact: medium.** Physical output.
- **Readiness:** ready. The owner relaxed the flash cap on 2026-09-25 (#149), so the faster speed is unblocked.

Follows #92 and complements #146.

title: Add a chase pattern that runs along connected Lines
body:
## Outcome and real setup

A light runs from Line to Line along the physical connections of the owner's Lines wall, following the shape instead of an axis or the center.

## Smallest useful implementation

- The worker needs the Lines connection topology.
- Today only the wall map owns connector geometry (`connector-geometry.json` is its drawing cache), and the worker must not read another owner's cache.
- First decide the source of topology: derive adjacency from zone and connector positions in the saved layout, or promote a topology owned by device state.
- Then add a `chase` pattern that orders Lines by a path walk.

## Behavior and protections to preserve

- The map's drawing cache ownership.
- The layout and device state specs.
- Free-only gating and the encoder bounds.

## Observable acceptance and planned evidence

- Topology fixture tests on the 15-Line layout, including a branching point.
- Chase frames step along adjacency.
- Bounds tests.
- Live check when requested.

## Meaningful deferrals

- Branch handling (split into both branches, or pick one) is decided in the design. Default: light both branches.


## Work assessment

Planning assessment, 2026-09-25, from #92's delivery and the live session. Source-only delivery unless stated.

- **Complexity: medium.** A new geometry input across the device state and worker boundary.
- **Uncertainty: medium.** The topology source is a design decision.
- **Impact: medium.**
- **Readiness:** backlog. Needs a topology-ownership decision, probably worth a short ADR.

Follows #92 and complements #146.

title: Offer a mood library of named animation presets
body:
## Outcome and real setup

When asked for something like "cozy", "ocean", "sunset", "aurora", "campfire" or "forest", Codex picks from a curated library of named presets (pattern, colors, speed, direction) instead of improvising palettes.

## Smallest useful implementation

- A static preset table in `bridge/effects.py`, reported by the animation options route and `nanoleaf_animations_list`.
- `animation.play` accepts either explicit fields or `preset: <name>`, resolved server-side to the same encoded effect.
- Start with about 8 presets.

## Behavior and protections to preserve

- Explicit animation requests keep working unchanged.
- Presets must pass the frame and byte bounds. No flash cap applies (owner decision in #149).
- The extension snapshot shape stays unchanged.

## Observable acceptance and planned evidence

- Every preset validates and renders within bounds.
- A preset request produces the same frames as the equivalent explicit request.
- MCP lists the presets.
- The owner reviews the palettes live when requested.

## Meaningful deferrals

- User-defined presets belong to #154.

title: Save and replay favorite animations by name
body:

title: Save a requested animation as a Nanoleaf scene
body:
## Outcome and real setup

An animation the owner likes can be saved on the Lines as a real Nanoleaf scene, so it appears in the Nanoleaf app and can be selected from a phone.

## Smallest useful implementation

- Use the Nanoleaf effect write commands to add, update and delete saved scenes. `add` stores the encoded display effect under a chosen name.
- This changes a standing rule in the bridge guide: no saved Nanoleaf scenes are added, edited or deleted.
- The owner authorized this on 2026-09-25 (see Decision below). Record the policy change in an ADR and in the bridge guide. Settle in the design: naming, collision handling, and how discovery then advertises the new scene.

## Behavior and protections to preserve

- Editing or deleting a scene happens only on an explicit request that names that scene. There is no bulk or implied deletion, and the remembered scene is never changed as a side effect.
- The remembered-scene policy.
- The single writer.
- Scene IDs stay opaque in shared v1.

## Observable acceptance and planned evidence

- A fake-device test of the `add` payload.
- A collision refusal test.
- Discovery picks up the new scene.
- A live check that it shows in the Nanoleaf app, when requested.

## Meaningful deferrals

- None beyond the design questions above.


## Work assessment

Planning assessment, 2026-09-25, from #92's delivery and the live session. Source-only delivery unless stated.

- **Complexity: medium.**
- **Uncertainty: medium.** The policy is decided. The firmware behavior of `add`, update and delete for custom effects is unverified; the first delivery step is a bounded live qualification, which needs the owner's go-ahead for device writes at that time.
- **Impact: high.** It writes persistent data on the device that the user also manages.
- **Readiness:** backlog. It is ready to plan once a qualification step is scheduled.

## Decision (owner, 2026-09-25)

The bridge may add, edit and delete scenes on the owner's Nanoleaf device. This replaces the bridge guide's rule that no saved scenes are added, edited or deleted, for this capability.

Follows #92 and complements #146.

title: Play requested animations on the NL22 Light Panels
body:
## Outcome and real setup

The same animations can play on the NL22 Light Panels, laid out from their triangle geometry.

## Smallest useful implementation

- Extend `effects.render` to Panels' one-zone triangles.
- Address the Panels device through the protected APIs.
- #92 excluded Panels, and the device-worker spec keeps protected APIs on Lines only, so this needs #113 first.

## Behavior and protections to preserve

- Per-device writers.
- The Panels' own mode and scene state.
- Lines behavior unchanged.

## Observable acceptance and planned evidence

- Encoder tests on the synthetic NL22 fixture.
- Admission tests addressing Panels.

title: Play hub moments as interludes on the Lines, then restore the current presentation
body:
## Outcome and real setup

A hub moment briefly plays on the Lines as an *interlude*, then returns to what is showing now: Work status, the remembered scene, or the Free content. This covers both "play this for 30 seconds, then restore" and event moments such as a merged PR.

This is the Nanoleaf side of the hub-decides/devices-guarantee plan in jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub#291. It was reshaped on 2026-09-25 from "Play an animation for a set time, then restore".

## Smallest useful implementation

- Implement the `moment` command from the shared contract release, jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub#292. Resolve its mood and palette to a Lines preset (#153), or render the palette with the requested pattern.
- The Lines worker saves the current base presentation, plays at most one interlude, and restores the current base when it ends.
- Any explicit command, a red or yellow alert, or a mode change ends the interlude early.
- Skip interludes in Quiet.
- Stopping and restoring the scene reuses #150's path.

## Behavior and protections to preserve

- One writer.
- Alerts always win.
- Completed comets are never restarted, and task pulse epochs are kept.
- No restore of a stale snapshot, and no replay after a restart.
- The remembered scene and brightness are unchanged.

## Observable acceptance and planned evidence

Fake-clock tests cover:
- interlude then restore, in Work and in Free;
- pre-emption by an alert;
- a mode change mid-interlude;
- restart mid-interlude, with no replay and a correct base;
- a duplicate idempotency key.

The shared conformance cases pass. There is a live check when requested.

## Meaningful deferrals

- Stacking or queuing several interludes: newest wins, and the rest are dropped with a receipt.

## Work assessment

- **Complexity: medium.** Scheduled state in the worker.
- **Uncertainty: medium** until the hub ADR and contract settle.
- **Impact: medium.**
- **Readiness:** backlog. The decision (jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub#291) and the contract (jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub#292) are delivered; pin [`controller-contracts-v1.1.0`](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/releases/tag/controller-contracts-v1.1.0) and read the adopter notes on jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub#292.

title: Investigate Codex sessions left blocked by MCP tool approvals
body:
## Observed

- During the #92 live check (2026-09-25), two `codex exec --ephemeral` sessions that called Nanoleaf MCP control tools ended normally.
- The shared feed kept them with an `approval` attention and unknown activity, so Nanoleaf showed them as blocked.
- In Work they would have lit red Lines for sessions that no longer exist.
- They were cleared with local Evict on both devices.

## Question and stop condition

- Where does the unresolved approval attention come from: the Codex hook events for MCP tool approval, the hub's shared monitor, or ephemeral sessions never emitting an end?
- Stop when the owning repository and the event sequence are identified, with a reproduction.
- Hand the fix to that owner (this repository or agent-device-hub).

## Behavior and protections to preserve

- Real approval requests must keep showing as blocked.
- Do not suppress alerts on the consumer side to hide an owner-side issue.

## Evidence to gather

- Replay one `codex exec` with an MCP control tool while capturing hook events and the shared feed.
- Compare with an interactive session.


## Work assessment

Planning assessment, 2026-09-25, from #92's delivery and the live session. Source-only delivery unless stated.

title: Document the in-place runtime upgrade, the codex exec MCP override and the hand-listed bridge modules
body:
Owner: `docs/development.md`, `docs/local-mcp.md`, the bridge guide.

## Outcome and real setup

Three things every recent Nanoleaf delivery rediscovered are written down. The #139, #92 and #44 closeouts on 2026-09-25 each proposed them for the docs and none landed.

Setup: the Linux runtime under `~/.local/share/codex-nanoleaf`, the repository docs. Excluded: the upgrade command itself (#140), code changes.

## Smallest useful implementation

- `docs/development.md`: an "Upgrade the installed runtime in place" section describing the guarded pattern used by gh-108, #139 and #92: back up, stop the services in order, replace only the changed files, restart, confirm the workers came back. Under shared input the device workers never exit on their own, so an upgrade must stop them. Point at the #139 install script kept in evidence as the reference until #140 replaces it.
- `docs/local-mcp.md`: the `codex exec` MCP override pattern used for the #92 live check, including that `codex exec` needs `< /dev/null` or it waits on stdin, and that ephemeral runs calling control tools leave "blocked" sessions in the hub feed (#160).
- Bridge guide or `docs/development.md`: `tests/test_prism_assets.py` and `tests/test_controller_cli.py` hand-list the bridge modules they copy, so a new bridge import must be added to both (bit #143 and #44 on the same day). Also `page.route('**/api/state')` does not match query strings, and `isHidden()` is true inside the closed Options menu, so assert the `hidden` attribute.

## Behavior and protections to preserve

- Fresh-install instructions, credentials handling and the private-state rules are unchanged.
- Nothing here authorizes an upgrade; it documents the procedure the owner has already run.

## Observable acceptance and planned evidence

Delivery target: source-only, one docs PR.

1. Each item appears in the named document with the trigger and the fix.
2. `python3 scripts/check.py` and the workflow checks exit zero.
3. Independent Standards and Specification reviews; guarded squash merge.

## Meaningful deferrals
